title: Enterprise tech deep dive - latency monitoring / regression detection
topics: How Redwood detects performance regressions in production
Slice dimensions: model, region, GPU SKU, runtime build, scheduler mode, kernel id
Alerting, paging hygiene, maintenance windows, deploy annotations
Customer visibility/roadmap for surfacing perf regression signals
Security/logging retention considerations for canary traffic
summary: Northstar Financial asked for a deep dive on how Redwood monitors latency/throughput drift over time and how regressions are detected and triaged. Redwood walked through internal production perf-canary approach (continuous low-footprint synthetic workload per region/model) and how it computes stable p95 latency and tokens/sec time series with warmup handling, cache priming, and minimum sample size. Discussed baseline options (rolling 7d median vs pinned known-good runtime build), deploy-window suppression and annotations, and what debug context is attached to alerts (runtime build/sha, GPU SKU, scheduler mode, kernel selection/fallback reason, batch stats). Customer requested clarity on how this could be surfaced to them during a pilot (webhook/Console view) and how canary traffic is isolated from customer queues. Next steps include sharing a one-pager/screenshots of internal dashboards, running a short Dedicated pilot with their prompt shapes, and a follow-up on security/log retention + integration with their PagerDuty/Datadog.
questions: Can we get customer-facing notifications when Redwood sees a regression for our pinned model/region?
How do you avoid false positives during deploys, warm cache changes, or GPU fleet heterogeneity?
What exactly is included in the alert payload (build SHA, kernel id, scheduler settings, batch sizes)?
How is tokens/sec computed for streaming responses (first-token alignment)?
Can canary runs be executed on the same GPU SKU we’re assigned in Dedicated?
What’s the plan/timeline to surface regression signals in the Redwood Console?
action_items: Noah Patel: Send perf-canary overview + example alert payload (with redacted links) to Northstar Financial by 2026-02-05
Logan Wright: Confirm which metric labels are safe to expose externally (cardinality + privacy) and propose a minimal customer-facing schema by 2026-02-10
Paula Mendes: Draft pilot success criteria (p95 latency + tokens/sec guardrails) for Northstar’s top 2 workloads by 2026-02-07
Priya Desai: Share representative prompt shapes (input token percentiles, max output, streaming vs non-streaming split) by 2026-02-06
Alex Romero: Provide Northstar’s preferred alert integration targets (PagerDuty service / Datadog monitors / webhook endpoint) by 2026-02-06
Evan Brooks: Send Northstar logging/retention requirements (30/90/180 day expectations, access controls) by 2026-02-06
next_steps: Redwood to share dashboard screenshots and a sample regression incident timeline (deploy annotation -> alert -> rollback).
Northstar to share prompt/token distribution and target regions so Redwood can propose the initial canary workload matrix for the pilot.
Schedule a follow-up (45 min) to review pilot plan + alerting integration details and security requirements.
If aligned, start a Dedicated pilot in us-east with a pinned runtime build and two models; expand to eu-west after week 2.
transcript:
Meeting: Enterprise tech deep dive - latency monitoring / regression detection
Recorded: 2026-02-03 17:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees:
- Noah Patel (Redwood Inference)
- Paula Mendes (Redwood Inference)
- Logan Wright (Redwood Inference)
- Priya Desai (Northstar Financial)
- Alex Romero (Northstar Financial)
- Dana Kim (Northstar Financial)
- Evan Brooks (Northstar Financial)

Auto-Summary (Fireflies): Customer evaluating Redwood Dedicated. Focus on how Redwood detects performance regressions (p95 latency + tokens/sec) and whether signals can be surfaced to customer. Discussed internal production canary, baseline strategy, alerting, and mitigation/rollback.


[00:00] Noah Patel: Cool. Uh, thanks everyone for the time. This one’s meant to be technical, so please interrupt. I’m Noah, I work on runtime performance on the inference side.

[00:10] Paula Mendes: Hey all, Paula here. I’m on product/requirements for some of the rollout and canary standards.

[00:15] Logan Wright: Logan. I’m telemetry/metrics side. So if we start arguing about labels and PromQL, that’s on me.

[00:22] Priya Desai: Great. Priya, platform eng. We’re basically trying to not get surprised. We’ve had… I don’t know, three incidents in six months where a model endpoint gets slower after a change and it takes too long to prove it’s real.

[00:36] Alex Romero: Alex, SRE. I care about like, does this page us at 2 AM and is it actionable.

[00:42] Dana Kim: Dana, applied ML. Our teams tend to change prompts and sometimes we change models. So I’m also curious what a “regression” even means in that context.

[00:50] Evan Brooks: Evan, security. I’ll mostly listen but I do have questions on what you log, retention, and whether canary prompts could leak anything.

[01:00] Noah Patel: Perfect. Maybe to start, could you share what you do today for latency monitoring? Like are you using Datadog APM, Grafana, in-house canaries?

[01:10] Priya Desai: Yeah, so we run our own Prometheus and Grafana. Some services are in Datadog too. For LLM, currently we use a mix of Azure OpenAI and one self-hosted vLLM cluster. We have synthetic checks but they’re kind of naive, it’s like one prompt every five minutes, and it doesn’t capture tokens per second.

[01:30] Alex Romero: And the killer is p95. Mean looks fine. But we care about tail. We have a p95 target of 1.8 seconds for our chat UI first token, and then like steady streaming. When it drifts, the product complains.

[01:46] Noah Patel: Got it. And do you have regions? Like multi-region active-active?

[01:50] Priya Desai: us-east and eu-west, yes. Data residency constraints for some workloads.

[01:56] Noah Patel: Okay. The way Redwood thinks about this is basically two complementary systems: offline benchmark lab (controlled) and a prod canary (messy reality). What you’re asking is more the latter.

[02:10] Dana Kim: When you say canary, you mean like a runtime canary build? Or a workload canary?

[02:15] Noah Patel: Workload canary. A small service that continuously runs representative inference requests against the production stack, tagged as canary traffic, so we can see performance drift with the exact fleet, kernel picks, scheduler heuristics, and so on.

[02:30] Paula Mendes: And to be clear, today it’s internal. It pages our oncall, not customers. But we’re actively designing it so it can be surfaced later, at least for Dedicated customers.

[02:40] Alex Romero: Okay. So what’s “representative” mean? Because our prompts vary a lot.

[02:45] Noah Patel: Totally. In v1 we pick a workload matrix that covers the main shapes that are sensitive: prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy, and streaming vs non-streaming. So for example: input 1k tokens output 128; input 4k output 32; input 200 output 800. That kind of thing. And we run it per model, per region, and we slice by GPU SKU.

[03:10] Logan Wright: And we keep it intentionally small. Like, not enough volume to contend with customer traffic. It uses a “canary-safe” request class with strict rate limit and priority controls.

[03:22] Priya Desai: Can you say more about the “slice by GPU” thing? We’ve gotten bitten by heterogenous nodes.

[03:28] Noah Patel: Yeah. In our fleet we may have multiple SKUs in a region (e.g., H100 vs A100 class), or even within an SKU there’s variance due to thermal or neighbor noise. We try not to smear. So the canary emits metrics with labels: model, region, gpu_sku, runtime_build, scheduler_mode, and then a few more like streaming=true/false.

[03:52] Logan Wright: With a caveat: we can’t label everything. Cardinality explodes. So we whitelist dimensions and aggregate at the right layer. Kernel id, for example, we do as debug context in the alert payload rather than a high-cardinality metric label in the main timeseries.

[04:08] Alex Romero: That’s interesting. So how do you compute p95? Like, are you computing p95 inside the runtime or in metrics backend?

[04:16] Logan Wright: Great question. We record per-request observations (histograms) and compute percentiles from histograms in the metrics system. For the canary specifically we also track sample size and enforce minimum N before we trust a percentile.

[04:30] Noah Patel: And we split latency into a couple pieces. Most customers care about time-to-first-token for streaming, and end-to-end for non-streaming. We track both.

[04:40] Dana Kim: Tokens per second is tricky. How do you measure that for streaming?

[04:45] Noah Patel: Yeah, we learned that one the hard way. For streaming we align tokens/sec to the first-token timestamp, not request start, otherwise you’re mixing prefill and networking jitter and it looks terrible. There was literally a bug we fixed where it was using request start and caused false regressions.

[05:05] Priya Desai: That’s exactly what we see. Our first-token latency is huge variance.

[05:10] Noah Patel: Right. So we treat it separately: TTFT p95 is one metric, and decode throughput tokens/sec is another.

[05:20] Alex Romero: Okay. Now, regression detection. How do you decide it’s a regression and not noise?

[05:28] Paula Mendes: We use baselines. Two modes. One is rolling baseline, like last 7 days median at the same time-of-day window. The other is pinned “known-good” build, especially around releases.

[05:42] Noah Patel: And we also suppress around deploy windows. Like if we’re rolling a new runtime version, for X minutes we’ll annotate and either reduce sensitivity or don’t page.

[05:55] Alex Romero: That’s important. Otherwise it’s pager spam.

[06:00] Logan Wright: The alert itself is “regression vs baseline” semantics. It includes observed p95, baseline p95, delta percent, plus the number of samples. If N is too low, it won’t page; it might open a low-priority ticket.

[06:16] Priya Desai: What are the thresholds? Like do you page at 5% regression or 20%?

[06:22] Paula Mendes: In v1 we’ve been conservative. Think like 10–15% sustained over 15–30 minutes for paging, depending on model. Throughput drops sometimes we treat separately. We tune per model family because some are noisier.

[06:40] Noah Patel: And to Alex’s point, we try to make it actionable. The payload includes: runtime_version, git SHA, GPU SKU, region, model id, scheduler mode, batch stats (like average batch size, prefill/decode counts), and a kernel selection summary.

[07:00] Evan Brooks: Kernel selection summary meaning what exactly? Is that like the operator kernel that got chosen? And is that logged somewhere?

[07:07] Noah Patel: It’s a debug export we gate behind canary tag. So only for canary requests, the runtime can emit “selected kernel id” and “fallback reason” if it didn’t pick the fast path. It’s not in customer logs by default.

[07:22] Logan Wright: And it’s not a super high-frequency log line either. We sample it. Otherwise it’d be noisy and costly.

[07:30] Evan Brooks: And prompts for the canary, those are synthetic, right? Not derived from customer data?

[07:35] Paula Mendes: Correct. We use a curated prompt set that contains no customer content. It’s like lorem-ish but shaped to hit token distributions. We can also incorporate customer-provided prompts in a pilot, but it would be explicitly agreed and stored in your boundary depending on deployment type.

[07:55] Dana Kim: For us, we could provide anonymized prompt templates. But we’d need controls.

[08:00] Noah Patel: Yep. For Dedicated, we can keep it in your dedicated environment. For Private (VPC/on-prem), it’s fully inside your network.

[08:12] Priya Desai: So stepping back, you said this is internal right now. If we’re in a pilot, can we see any of this?

[08:20] Paula Mendes: Not as a polished product, but yes we can share dashboards during the pilot and we can set up notification flows. For example, a webhook when a regression is detected for your dedicated cluster, or a shared Slack channel where our oncall posts the context. Longer term, we’re planning to surface it in the Redwood Console.

[08:42] Alex Romero: We’d want PagerDuty integration ideally. Or at least something we can route.

[08:47] Logan Wright: Technically feasible. The trick is avoiding flooding you. We’d likely start with “ticket-first” severity and then graduate to paging once tuned.

[08:58] Noah Patel: Also, since it’s a pilot, we can pin runtime builds. That helps. If you keep runtime_build constant, any regression is more likely due to fleet or model version changes rather than code change.

[09:12] Dana Kim: But we might change prompts or max tokens. How do you control for that?

[09:18] Noah Patel: For canary, we control prompts. So it’s measuring the platform, not your evolving application. Separately, your app metrics can measure what users experience. Think of canary as “engine health.”

[09:32] Priya Desai: That’s helpful framing.

[09:35] Alex Romero: So what’s the isolation story? You said “canary-safe.” We’ve seen canaries ironically cause contention.

[09:42] Noah Patel: Totally fair. We implement canary requests in a separate priority class with strict QPS ceiling and a cap on concurrent requests. It cannot starve customer queues. In fact it yields to customer traffic.

[09:58] Logan Wright: And we monitor overhead. There’s a “noise budget” report we run: does canary sampling add measurable CPU overhead, metric emission overhead, etc.

[10:08] Priya Desai: Okay. Can you walk through what a real regression looks like? Like, what would you see, what do you do.

[10:16] Noah Patel: Sure. Example from staging: tokens/sec dropped ~18% for one model in eu-west on A100 only. Alert included runtime build diff and kernel selection changed from kernel_42 to fallback_13 due to sequence length distribution crossing a threshold. We correlated with a runtime deploy. We rolled back that build while investigating. The canary made it obvious it wasn’t general networking.

[10:45] Alex Romero: That’s exactly what we want. “It’s this GPU and this build.”

[10:50] Logan Wright: The dashboard has a heatmap view too: model vs region, color-coded by regression magnitude. Then drill down to GPU SKU.

[11:00] Priya Desai: This sounds like what some providers claim, but they don’t show details. Bedrock gives you CloudWatch but it’s opaque.

[11:10] Noah Patel: Right, and we’re not perfect either, but the goal is speed to attribution.

[11:18] Dana Kim: How do you choose baseline? Rolling baseline can hide slow drift if it’s constantly updating.

[11:25] Paula Mendes: Yep. That’s the tradeoff. Rolling baseline is good for day/night patterns. Pinned baseline is good for detecting drift relative to known-good. We often do both: rolling for “is it weird today” and pinned for “did this release regress vs last release.”

[11:45] Alex Romero: And suppressions? Maintenance windows.

[11:49] Logan Wright: We support explicit maintenance windows. Also deploy annotations. If a region is mid-roll, we can silence paging but still record the metrics. And we keep the annotation so later you can see “this change happened here.”

[12:05] Priya Desai: Okay. What about caching effects? KV cache warming, prefix cache.

[12:11] Noah Patel: That’s a big source of variance. Canary runs have warmup steps. We do an initial warm run that we exclude from stats, and optionally a cache priming step so each measurement is more consistent.

[12:25] Dana Kim: Doesn’t that hide regressions related to cold-start?

[12:28] Noah Patel: Great callout. It can. So we usually track both: cold-ish TTFT and warm steady-state. But in v1 we prioritize stable signal for regression detection. Cold-start is more like a separate SLO.

[12:45] Alex Romero: For us, cold start matters less because we keep capacity warm. But during incidents it spikes.

[12:51] Noah Patel: Understood.

[13:00] Evan Brooks: On logs and metrics retention, what’s your default? And can we control it?

[13:06] Paula Mendes: For Dedicated and Private we can align with your retention requirements. The canary prompts themselves are synthetic, but metrics may still include model id, region, etc. We can scope who has access. We have audit logs for access and changes.

[13:25] Logan Wright: And for external exposure, we’d likely only expose aggregated metrics. Not raw request logs. That keeps privacy and cardinality manageable.

[13:38] Priya Desai: Makes sense.

[13:40] Noah Patel: Can I ask: what’s your success criteria for a pilot, on the monitoring front?

[13:46] Priya Desai: Two things. One, we need confidence that if latency regresses, you detect it faster than our users do. Two, we need enough context to know whether to escalate to you or it’s on our side.

[14:02] Alex Romero: And I need to know that we won’t get spammed with false positives. Like, if it’s one node having issues, I want it aggregated in a sane way.

[14:11] Noah Patel: Yep. We do outlier filtering at the node level sometimes, but we’re cautious not to hide real problems. Mostly we address that by slicing. If one GPU SKU is weird, it shows up as that slice.

[14:28] Dana Kim: Our concern is also model upgrades. If we swap from Model A to Model B, our tokens/sec changes. How do you separate “expected change” vs “regression”?

[14:38] Paula Mendes: In rollout policy, model changes are annotated too. The canary can be pinned to a specific model version, so you can compare apples to apples. And for your app, you’d track quality/latency across A/B.

[14:55] Noah Patel: Also canary’s job is not to say “your product got slower” in the absolute sense. It’s to say “the serving stack for this model+hardware got slower relative to itself.”

[15:10] Priya Desai: Okay. Let’s talk details: what metrics exactly would we see in a dashboard?

[15:16] Logan Wright: For canary we typically show:
- TTFT p95 (streaming)
- End-to-end latency p95 (non-streaming)
- Decode tokens/sec (streaming)
- Overall tokens/sec (non-streaming)
- Request success rate
- Sample count
And then drill-down panels for batch size distribution, queue time, GPU utilization (if available), and “recent deploy” annotations.

[15:45] Alex Romero: Queue time as in scheduler queue?

[15:48] Noah Patel: Yes. We instrument scheduler queue depth and time-in-queue for canary requests. But again, we isolate it so it should reflect system state without adding load.

[16:02] Priya Desai: What about p99? We care about p95 mostly but p99 sometimes reveals a tail issue.

[16:08] Logan Wright: We can show p99 too. The challenge is sample size. For synthetic low-volume canary, p99 can be noisy. So we tend to page on p95 and use p99 for investigation.

[16:25] Alex Romero: That’s consistent with our experience.

[16:28] Noah Patel: Another thing is we attach links in the alert. Like direct link to dashboard filtered to that model/region/GPU and a link to a runbook.

[16:40] Priya Desai: Do you actually have a runbook? Like step-by-step?

[16:44] Noah Patel: Yes. First steps are basically: confirm sample size, check if deploy annotation happened, compare slices (GPU SKU, region), look for kernel selection changes, and then decide rollback vs deeper profiling.

[16:58] Paula Mendes: And we’re making those runbooks consistent with our general oncall process.

[17:05] Evan Brooks: Profiling—does that mean you capture traces or something? Any sensitive data concerns?

[17:12] Noah Patel: For canary we can capture profiler traces because the prompts are synthetic. For customer traffic we don’t capture raw payloads. For Dedicated we can do opt-in profiling if you agree.

[17:30] Dana Kim: Okay. I want to bring up something: streaming user experience. Sometimes the first token is okay, but then it slows down mid-stream.

[17:40] Noah Patel: That’s why we measure decode throughput separately. We also track variance in tokens/sec over a response. In v1 we mostly do average decode tokens/sec, but we can add “chunk cadence” metrics later.

[17:58] Priya Desai: That would be useful.

[18:00] Noah Patel: Maybe we should align on what models you’re evaluating. Are you planning on open models or…?

[18:06] Dana Kim: Mostly open. We’re comparing a couple: like a 70B-ish class, and maybe a smaller reranker/embedding model. We care about dedicated GPUs because of predictable performance.

[18:20] Noah Patel: Great. For the canary, we’d focus on that 70B class model in us-east and eu-west. Then add one smaller model later.

[18:30] Alex Romero: And GPU type? We’d want H100 ideally.

[18:34] Noah Patel: For Dedicated we can provision consistent GPU SKU. That actually makes regression detection easier.

[18:43] Logan Wright: Also reduces the need for slicing.

[18:45] Priya Desai: What about autoscaling? If it scales up/down, performance changes.

[18:50] Noah Patel: Yep. Autoscaling introduces variance. For canary we can pin to a stable small capacity pool or at least annotate scaling events so you can correlate.

[19:05] Paula Mendes: The roadmap is to integrate these perf regressions with our rollout system. So when a rollout happens (runtime or model), canary results become a gate/health signal.

[19:18] Priya Desai: That’s interesting. So you’d stop a rollout if canary regresses?

[19:22] Paula Mendes: Internally, yes—that’s where we’re heading. Today it’s more “alert and rollback manually.”

[19:30] Alex Romero: That’s basically what we do but we don’t have the signal.

[19:34] Noah Patel: Exactly.

[19:38] Dana Kim: On the baseline: last 7 days median—do you account for weekday vs weekend patterns?

[19:44] Logan Wright: We can. Easiest is rolling 7d at same hour. But in practice, since canary is isolated, the biggest patterns are deploys and fleet changes, not diurnal traffic.

[19:58] Alex Romero: Unless the cluster is shared.

[20:00] Noah Patel: For Hosted API, yes, there’s more shared contention. For Dedicated, much less.

[20:06] Priya Desai: We’re leaning Dedicated, so that helps.

[20:10] Evan Brooks: Dedicated still uses your control plane, right? Any cross-tenant metrics issues?

[20:15] Paula Mendes: Dedicated has isolation at the compute pool and data plane. Control plane is shared but requests and data stay isolated. Metrics access is RBAC’d.

[20:28] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[20:30] Noah Patel: Let’s talk about what you’d want surfaced. Priya asked “can we see it.” In a pilot, we can share a dashboard view. Longer term, we envision a Console page where you can see per-model per-region p95 and tokens/sec, with annotations.

[20:48] Priya Desai: Would that be internal to Redwood or accessible to us?

[20:52] Paula Mendes: The internal one exists. The customer-facing one is roadmap. But for a pilot, we can provide read-only access to a scoped dashboard or export metrics via an integration.

[21:05] Alex Romero: Export is ideal. We want it in our Grafana.

[21:10] Logan Wright: That’s doable if we define a stable schema. The concern is label explosion. But we can keep it to: model, region, gpu_sku, and maybe runtime_build.

[21:22] Noah Patel: And we could send you events instead of raw timeseries: “regression detected” events with context and links.

[21:30] Alex Romero: That might actually be better for paging.

[21:34] Priya Desai: Agree. We don’t need every metric, we need the “something changed.”

[21:40] Dana Kim: Plus, if it’s a model change we did, we don’t want you paging us.

[21:45] Noah Patel: Exactly. We can scope to platform regressions.

[21:50] Priya Desai: Another question: how do you ensure the canary isn’t biased by batching? Like if scheduler decides to batch differently, tokens/sec changes.

[21:58] Noah Patel: Great point. We do two things. One: we pin scheduler mode for canary runs, so it uses a stable scheduling configuration. Two: we emit batch composition stats so we can tell if the batcher changed behavior.

[22:15] Logan Wright: Batch stats are super helpful because otherwise you see “tokens/sec down” but it’s actually “average batch size shrank.”

[22:25] Alex Romero: Right.

[22:28] Priya Desai: Pinning scheduler mode—does that reflect reality though?

[22:33] Noah Patel: It’s a tradeoff. Pinning reduces variance, increases attribution. But it may miss regressions that only happen in the mixed customer scheduler mode. So we typically run two canaries: one “pinned stable” and one “realistic shared.” V1 may start with pinned.

[22:56] Dana Kim: That seems reasonable.

[23:00] Evan Brooks: Any compliance concerns with running synthetic traffic? Like does it show up in audits?

[23:06] Paula Mendes: It’s internal operational traffic, tagged and auditable. It’s also rate-limited. We can document it for your audit package.

[23:18] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[23:20] Noah Patel: Let’s check: what do you consider a meaningful regression? Alex said p95 TTFT target 1.8 seconds. Is a 10% bump meaningful?

[23:30] Alex Romero: Yeah, 10% sustained is meaningful. But we’d probably want to page only if it’s like, 15%+ or crosses a hard threshold.

[23:40] Priya Desai: For tokens/sec, if it drops 10% users notice.

[23:45] Noah Patel: Okay. That aligns with our current policies.

[23:50] Dana Kim: And for a 70B model, what tokens/sec should we expect? Roughly.

[23:56] Noah Patel: Depends on GPU and context length, but we can share expected ranges once we know your token shapes. We usually avoid promising a single number without workload definition.

[24:10] Priya Desai: Fair.

[24:12] Noah Patel: One more question: how fast do you need detection? Like 5 minutes vs 30 minutes.

[24:18] Alex Romero: Ideally under 15 minutes. The longer it goes, the more user impact.

[24:24] Noah Patel: That’s consistent. We generally compute over rolling windows like 10–15 minutes with min sample size.

[24:35] Logan Wright: And we use sustained condition: it has to persist across multiple evaluation windows.

[24:42] Priya Desai: Okay.

[24:45] Noah Patel: Should we talk about integration with your stack? You said Prometheus/Grafana.

[24:52] Priya Desai: Yeah. We can ingest webhooks and we can also pull from an API. But simplest might be: you alert internally, and you notify us if it’s affecting our dedicated environment.

[25:05] Alex Romero: I’d want at least an email/slack notification if Redwood sees something. So we’re not blind.

[25:12] Paula Mendes: We can do that in a pilot.

[25:16] Dana Kim: One more thing: do you correlate regressions with code changes? Like do you auto-link to PRs.

[25:22] Noah Patel: For internal yes. We attach “last runtime deploy” metadata: version and SHA, and we can link to deploy diff. For customer we probably won’t link to internal PRs, but we can say “runtime_build changed from X to Y at time T.”

[25:40] Priya Desai: That’s enough.

[25:42] Alex Romero: And rollback—do you roll back automatically?

[25:46] Noah Patel: Not automatically in v1. But we can roll back quickly. For Dedicated, we can keep a known-good runtime ready.

[25:58] Paula Mendes: Longer-term, automatic rollback is on the roadmap once confidence is high.

[26:05] Priya Desai: Okay.

[26:08] Evan Brooks: Can you share where these dashboards live? Is it Grafana? And what’s access control.

[26:14] Logan Wright: Internally it’s Grafana. Access is through SSO/RBAC. For pilot, we’d likely share screenshots or set up a scoped view. We’d need to align with our internal policies.

[26:30] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[26:32] Noah Patel: I think we’ve hit most of it. Maybe we should define next steps. From our side, we can send a one-pager on the perf canary, plus an example alert payload so you can see the fields.

[26:45] Priya Desai: Yes, please. And we’ll send you our token distribution.

[26:50] Dana Kim: I can provide like p50/p90 input tokens, output tokens, and streaming split.

[26:56] Noah Patel: Perfect.

[27:00] Alex Romero: And for alerting integration, I’ll send what PagerDuty service we’d want, or if we want to start in slack.

[27:08] Paula Mendes: Great. We can start with Slack/email and then move to PagerDuty once tuned.

[27:15] Logan Wright: Also, if you want it in Grafana, we can talk about a minimal external schema. I’ll take that as a follow-up.

[27:24] Priya Desai: Okay.

[27:26] Noah Patel: Before we end, any concerns or objections? Like, is there anything that would block you from a pilot?

[27:32] Evan Brooks: I’d need your security docs and retention policy, especially around metrics and logs. Not worried about synthetic prompts, but access control matters.

[27:44] Paula Mendes: Understood. We’ll coordinate with our security team and send the relevant docs.

[27:50] Dana Kim: For me, I’d want to see that tokens/sec measurement is correct, especially streaming. We’ve been burned.

[27:56] Noah Patel: We can demonstrate it during pilot. And we can show how we compute it.

[28:02] Alex Romero: I’m mostly happy, but I’ll repeat: if this pages us for noise, it’s a non-starter.

[28:08] Noah Patel: Totally. We’ll start with non-paging notifications and tune. And our canary is designed to avoid false positives: min sample size, sustained windows, and deploy suppressions.

[28:22] Priya Desai: Sounds good.

[28:25] Noah Patel: Great. We’ll send follow-ups by end of week.

[28:30] (crosstalk)

[28:31] Paula Mendes: Thanks everyone.

[28:33] Logan Wright: Thank you.

[28:35] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[28:36] Alex Romero: Appreciate it.
